data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":{"adopted_commitment_refs":[],"disanalogies":["RFC 9110 idempotence is a classification of HTTP methods by their defined semantics; event-log deduplication is a runtime mechanism","RFC 9110 idempotence is claimed by the method specification; event-log idempotence must be enforced by the system infrastructure","HTTP safety includes a client-intent dimension; event-log deduplication is purely server-side"],"overturn_conditions":["If the problem's framing ('Drawing on published definitions') demands the RFC 9110 definitions be directly applied as the answer, this candidate is too dismissive of the analogy"],"shared_structure":["Both notions involve 'same result under repetition'","Both concern the behavior of a system when an operation is applied multiple times"],"source_memory_refs":["SRC_007"],"transfer_claims":["The RFC 9110 definitions provide conceptual scaffolding for understanding what the event log needs, but the actual requirement is a distinct operational property"]},"claim":"The append-only event log does not require idempotence in the RFC 9110 sense at all. RFC 9110 idempotence is a property of HTTP request methods defined over 'intended effect on the server,' which is a semantic, declarative notion. The event log requires operational deduplication \u2014 a mechanical guarantee that duplicate physical writes are collapsed \u2014 which is a distinct and stronger property. Conflating the two obscures the design problem.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If the problem explicitly asks for the RFC 9110 definition to be applied analogically (which it does: 'Drawing on published definitions'), then the operational-deduplication framing alone is insufficient and must be supplemented by the RFC 9110 distinction.","eval":"observation"},{"case":"If RFC 9110's definition of idempotence is sufficiently general (covering any operation, not just HTTP methods), then the layer distinction collapses.","eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"RFC 9110 idempotence says 'the intended effect of N identical requests equals the effect of 1.' This is a claim about the method's defined semantics, not a protocol-level mechanism. An event-log writer needs a concrete deduplication mechanism (e.g., monotonically increasing sequence numbers, content-addressed hashing, or client-assigned idempotency keys) to detect and suppress duplicates. This is an operational invariant, not an HTTP semantic classification. The two notions share the word 'idempotent' but refer to different abstraction layers.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
